title: Short Stuff: Mojave Megaphone
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Mojave Megaphone, a giant weathered steel megaphone-like object bolted to boulders on a hill in the Mojave Desert National Preserve, whose origin and purpose are unknown. The hosts walk through theories: a 1940s-50s siren or early warning signal (tied to nearby nuclear testing and military/air force activity, and a rail line carrying chemical agents), an old salt mine brine pipe or pipeline venturi, a rocket booster, an art installation, and a shock-wave detection device linked to Nevada nuclear testing. They note it has no markings, looks like a one-off handmade piece, is about eight feet long, and that tour operators estimate it has been there thirty or more years. They also give the coordinates, describe the four-wheel-drive access route, and mention a gold-treasure legend. Edwards Air Force Base and Chuck Yeager are mentioned as nearby context.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to the Mojave Megaphone
segments.summary: Hosts banter about driving through the Mojave Desert and introduce the mysterious giant steel megaphone in the Mojave Desert National Preserve.

segments.title: Description of the megaphone
segments.summary: The object is a weathered steel structure about eight feet long, bolted to boulders on a hill, with two rocket-booster-like halves mouth to mouth, triangular fins, rebar crosshairs inside, and no markings. It looks like a one-off handmade piece that took several people to install.

segments.title: Siren and early warning theories
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the idea that it was a siren from the 1940s or 1950s tied to nearby military and nuclear testing, and why this theory is doubted, including the remote location and the nearby rail line carrying chemical agents. They note WWII air raid sirens look similar but work better.

segments.title: Other theories: salt mine, venturi, art, detector
segments.summary: Theories include a salt mine brine pipe, a pipeline venturi, a rocket booster, an art installation, and a device that detected long-range shock waves from Nevada nuclear testing. A tour operator estimated it has been there thirty or more years, and the hosts note the lack of pipeline records.

segments.title: Access, coordinates, and gold legend
segments.summary: The hosts give the coordinates and warn that reaching the site requires a four-wheel-drive vehicle over dirt roads, sand, and canyons. They mention a legend that it points to buried gold, which they doubt, and mention Edwards Air Force Base and Chuck Yeager as nearby.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to get in touch with any visits or tests and close the episode, with a note about iHeartRadio.
